title: A Star for Every State

hero.credit: Emanuel Leutze, *Washington Crossing the Delaware*, 1851. The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Public domain.

objective: Students will learn that the flag began with **13 stars** for the 13 states that had been the Thirteen Colonies, and that a star was added for each state that joined, until there were **50**. They will count stars, put flags in order, read a list of states and years, and find their own state’s star.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: The flag has changed as the country grew. Every star has a story, and one of them is yours.

materials: The *Show your class* page (page 3), projected or printed
Crayons, including blue; the differentiated handouts
If you can, the exhibition’s *Add a Star* room on the screen
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** in *Add a Star*, start with 13 stars. Before each of the flag’s seven jumps, guess the decade a state joined; then its star goes on, with every state that joined before it. A bullseye scores 3 points; one decade out scores 1. Play it as a class, and cheer when your state’s star appears.

steps.title: How many stars?
script: Ask: *“How many stars are on our flag?”* Take guesses and write them on the board. Then ask what each star might stand for. Collect ideas before you tell: **each star stands for a state, and there are 50.** *“But the flag did not always have 50 stars. Today we will find out how it grew.”*

screen.question: How many stars are on our flag? What do you think each star stands for?

steps.purpose: Start from the flag students know, and guess before they are told.
students: What could a star stand for?

steps.title: A new constellation
script: Tell the beginning. *“In 1776, the Thirteen Colonies declared they were free: 13 new states. A year later, on June 14, 1777, the leaders decided what the flag would look like.”* Read their words slowly: “thirteen stars, white in a blue field representing a new constellation”. Ask what a constellation is: a group of stars that makes a picture in the sky. *“The 13 stars were a new picture: a new country.”*

June 14, 1777:
“thirteen stars, white in a blue field

steps.purpose: Hear how the flag began, and why it had 13 stars.

steps.title: How the flag grew
script: Show the four flags on page 3, one at a time, and read the chart. As states joined, stars were added. In **1795** there were 15 stars, and 15 stripes too: that is the flag of *The Star-Spangled Banner*. By **1818** there were 20 states, and the flag went back to 13 stripes, with a star for every state, added on the July 4 after the state joined. Hawaii was the 50th state; the 50-star flag became official on **July 4, 1960**.

steps.purpose: Read four flags in order, from 13 stars to 50.
students: Which flag had the most stripes?
When did the flag reach 50 stars?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students work on a handout. All three count the first flag’s stars, put flags in order and finish a flag of their own. Circulate and ask: *“How do you know which flag is older?”* More stars means later.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Count the first flag’s 13 stars, match two flags to their years, color the first flag, and trace 13 and 50.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Count stars and stripes on two flags, write the year under four flags in order, read a list of states and their stars, then draw a new constellation of 13.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Count on from 13 to 50 on a number line, fill in a table of the four flags, find their own state’s star in the full list, and say why a constellation is a good name.

steps.purpose: Count, order and find stars, at the right level for each student.
students: Every handout ends with a flag for you to finish.

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the questions on the screen. For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down: *“Can you now say what each star on the flag stands for? Can you now count the first flag’s stars, and say why there were 13? Can you now put the flags in order, from 13 stars to 50? Can you now find your state’s star?”* Ask a Red Level student to answer the last.

steps.title: Our state’s star
script: Then find your state together in the list on page 3. If it was one of the first 13, say so: it was there from the start. If it joined later, read its star and year, and count how many stars were already on the flag before it.

screen.question: Which star is our state? Was it one of the first 13?

steps.purpose: End with the star that belongs to the class: their own state.
students: Find our state in the list.
Was it one of the first 13, or did it join later?
